item.title: CISA Flags Exploited Langflow and ColdFusion Bugs as Ubiquiti, GhostLock Risks Emerge
item.content:encoded:
CISA orders feds to prioritize patching Langflow auth bypass flaw — Must Read

CISA ordered U.S. federal agencies to patch an actively exploited Langflow authorization bypass flaw, CVE-2026-55255, by Friday. Attackers are using the bug to access other users’ AI flows, steal sensitive data or credentials, and potentially deploy follow-on implants.

  • CISA gave U.S. federal agencies until Friday to patch CVE-2026-55255, an actively exploited vulnerability in the Langflow visual framework for building AI agents.
  • CVE-2026-55255 is an Insecure Direct Object Reference flaw that lets authenticated attackers access other users’ flows by sending a crafted request to the /api/v1/responses endpoint with a victim’s flow_id UUID.
  • Successful exploitation can allow attackers to access sensitive data processed by victims’ flows and consume their resources.
  • Sysdig’s Threat Research Team first observed exploitation of CVE-2026-55255 in the wild on June 25 and said the objective was code execution and second-stage implant delivery.
  • CISA added CVE-2026-55255 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and said this type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector that poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Ubiquiti warns of new max severity UniFi OS vulnerability — Must Read

Ubiquiti released patches for seven critical UniFi OS vulnerabilities, including a maximum-severity UniFi Connect command injection flaw that could let a network-accessible attacker execute commands on affected devices. Users should update UniFi Connect to version 3.4.20 or later and apply the latest UniFi OS application/device updates immediately.

  • Ubiquiti released security updates for seven critical vulnerabilities in UniFi OS, including the maximum-severity command injection flaw CVE-2026-50746.
  • CVE-2026-50746 affects UniFi Connect Application versions 3.4.16 and earlier, and Ubiquiti advised users to update to version 3.4.20 or later.
  • Ubiquiti also patched six additional critical-severity issues in UniFi Talk, UniFi Access, UniFi Protect, UniFi OS Server, and multiple Ubiquiti routers, gateways, NAS, and surveillance systems.
  • Ubiquiti has not disclosed whether any of the vulnerabilities were exploited before being fixed, but said six can be exploited in low-complexity attacks that do not require user interaction.
  • Censys tracks more than 100,000 UniFi OS instances exposed online, with nearly 50,000 IP addresses in the United States, though the data may include historical results and may not reflect current exposure.

CISA orders feds to patch max severity ColdFusion flaw by Friday — Must Read

CISA ordered U.S. federal agencies to patch an actively exploited maximum-severity Adobe ColdFusion flaw, CVE-2026-48282, by Friday because it can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. Adobe has already released fixes and warned administrators to deploy them immediately.

  • CISA ordered U.S. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to patch the actively exploited Adobe ColdFusion vulnerability CVE-2026-48282 by Friday, June 10.
  • CVE-2026-48282 affects Adobe ColdFusion versions 2025.9, 2023.20, and earlier, and can be exploited remotely without privileges in low-complexity attacks to gain code execution on unpatched systems.
  • Adobe released security updates one week before the article and urged administrators to install them immediately, saying the flaw posed a high risk of exploitation.
  • KEVIntel founder Ryan Dewhurst warned that attackers began exploiting CVE-2026-48282 within two hours of Adobe's disclosure, and the Canadian Center for Cyber Security encouraged defenders to secure their systems.
  • Shadowserver currently tracks nearly 800 Adobe ColdFusion instances exposed online, though it is unknown how many are honeypots or already secured against attacks targeting CVE-2026-48282.

China-Linked UAT-7810 Expands ORB Network With New LONGLEASH Malware — Must Read

China-linked UAT-7810 is expanding its LapDogs ORB network by compromising internet-facing routers and deploying newly developed malware including LONGLEASH, DOGLEASH, LEASHTEST, and JARLEASH. Cisco Talos says the group is actively refining its tooling to provide relay infrastructure that other China-nexus actors can use in attacks against high-value targets.

  • Cisco Talos reports that the Chinese threat actor UAT-7810 is refining bespoke malware to expand its LapDogs Operational Relay Box network by compromising internet-facing networking devices.
  • UAT-7810 is assessed as responsible for maintaining and proliferating the LapDogs network, which can be leveraged by associated secondary threat actors for attacks against high-value targets.
  • The group has developed a newer version of ShortLeash called LONGLEASH and has also used previously unreported tools named DOGLEASH, LEASHTEST, and JARLEASH.
  • UAT-7810 attack chains have weaponized known vulnerabilities in unpatched Ruckus wireless routers, including CVE-2020-22653, CVE-2020-22658, and CVE-2023-25717.
  • Campaigns observed earlier in the year targeted ASUS AiCloud routers vulnerable to CVE-2025-2492, indicating possible attempts to broaden the ORB network.

15-Year-Old GhostLock Flaw Enables Root and Container Escape on Most Linux Distros — Must Read

GhostLock (CVE-2026-43499) is a 15-year-old Linux kernel flaw that lets any local user gain root and escape containers on many unpatched distributions, with public exploit code now available. Administrators should urgently update to their distribution’s latest kernel, especially on shared, cloud, container, and CI systems.

  • Nebula Security disclosed GhostLock (CVE-2026-43499), a 15-year-old Linux kernel flaw that can let any logged-in user gain root control on an unpatched machine.
  • The vulnerable code has shipped by default in essentially every mainstream Linux distribution since 2011 and requires no special permission, unusual settings, or network access.
  • Nebula developed a working exploit that was 97% reliable in its testing, escapes containers, and took about five seconds on its test machine.
  • The flaw was fixed in April, but distributions are still rolling out patches, and the article says users should install their distribution’s current kernel rather than only the first patched build.
  • Nebula says GhostLock is the second half of its IonStack chain, where a Firefox flaw runs code inside the browser and escapes its sandbox while GhostLock provides root access.

UK Cybercrime Journal: SMS Blaster Gang Convicted — Should Read

UK police secured another conviction in an SMS Blaster smishing operation that used a rogue mobile mast-like device to spoof HMRC texts and target thousands of people in London. The case shows how criminals can bypass SMS safeguards locally, reinforcing the need to report suspicious texts and move away from SMS-based authentication.

  • The City of London Police’s Dedicated Card and Payment Crime Unit secured the conviction of Di Li for his role in an SMS Blaster fraud operation in London.
  • Ruichen Xiong drove around London between 22 and 27 March 2025 using an SMS Blaster to send fraudulent messages to tens of thousands of potential victims.
  • The fraudulent text messages purported to be from HMRC, and officers nearby received them while the device was operating in North London.
  • Investigators recovered digital evidence from Li’s home showing communications between Li and Xiong about deploying the SMS Blaster.
  • The article says SMS Blasters can force nearby phones to connect through a downgraded 2G connection, allowing criminals to send spoofed messages without needing victims’ phone numbers.

Inside the Underground Economy: 5 Dark Web Trends Shaping the 2026 Threat Landscape — Optional

The dark web has evolved into an operational hub for cybercrime in 2026, where ransomware groups, access brokers, stolen identities, geopolitical campaigns, and AI-enabled tools are traded and coordinated before attacks occur. Organizations need proactive dark web intelligence to detect exposed access and emerging threats before they are weaponized.

  • The article says the dark web has grown beyond a market for stolen credentials into an operational hub where ransomware services, initial network access, exploit kits, phishing infrastructure, and AI-powered attack tools are traded.
  • In March 2026, five ransomware operations—Qilin, Akira, The Gentlemen, DragonForce, and INC Ransom—were responsible for more than 56% of recorded ransomware activity.
  • Researchers observed 20 March 2026 listings advertising access to compromised corporate networks, with professional services accounting for 25% and retail accounting for 20% of those listings.
  • The article states that valid credentials, session hijacking, multi-factor authentication bypass techniques, and third-party access abuse have made identity a primary attack surface for enterprises.
  • During the February 2026 escalation in the Middle East, the article reports that internet connectivity in affected regions dropped to between 1% and 4% of normal levels, more than 70 hacktivist groups became active, over 8,000 conflict-themed domains were registered, and navigation disruptions affected more than 1,100 vessels near the Strait of Hormuz.
